passage: It was pouring, and the bus to the fair would leave in ten minutes. Ojas ran into his house with Harish behind him, both soaked. Ojas's grandmother came into the room. Ojas quickly bent and touched her feet, as he did each time. Harish, whose family did not do this, froze. He glanced at the clock and at her. Then he stood straight and joined his palms. “Namaste, Dadi.” She nodded warmly, patted his cheek and said, “Both are good. Go, go, the bus won't wait.” They ran out into the rain, laughing.

qa.q: How many minutes until the bus to the fair left?
qa.a: The bus would leave in ten minutes.

qa.q: What might Harish have been feeling when he froze, and what else might explain it?
qa.a: Probably unsure what to do, since his family does not touch feet, and rushed because of the bus. He may also have wanted to be respectful without copying wrongly.

qa.q: How did Ojas's grandmother handle the moment?
qa.a: She accepted Harish's namaste warmly and said both ways are good, so nobody felt wrong, and she sent them on their way.

qa.q: How might Ojas see Harish's greeting?
qa.a: As just a different family way, since they went off laughing and Ojas seems to see no problem.

grounding: Kneeling or touching feet is respect in some families and not others; different greetings can both be respectful.

passage: On her first day at the new school, Vasudha stayed in her seat when Parul Ma'am walked in. The rest of the class stood up and said, “Good morning, Ma'am.” Vasudha's cheeks went hot. She stood late, halfway. Parul Ma'am smiled and said, “In your old school it was probably different. Here we stand to greet the teacher. It isn't about being small, it is our way of saying hello.” At recess her new friend Sarika said, “You'll get used to it.” Next morning Vasudha was the first to stand.

qa.q: What did the class do when Parul Ma'am walked in?
qa.a: They stood up and said, “Good morning, Ma'am.”

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she stayed in her seat and then stood late?
qa.a: Embarrassed and unsure, since her cheeks went hot. She was also probably trying to learn a new custom.

qa.q: What did Parul Ma'am do that helped Vasudha?
qa.a: She stayed kind and explained that standing is a way of saying hello here, not a sign of being small, and she acknowledged that Vasudha's old school may be different.

qa.q: How might the other children have seen Vasudha staying seated?
qa.a: Possibly as surprising, but they may also just have thought she was new. Sarika's friendly words suggest they were welcoming.

grounding: Standing to greet a teacher is respect in that school culture; customs differ across schools and families.

passage: “Why did you jump up like that?” Usha giggled as her grandmother shuffled into the room with a plate of banana chips. Indu sat back down, cheeks warm. “At my house we always stand when an elder comes in. My Nanaji says it's respect.” “We don't. Ammachi would say sit, sit, don't make a fuss.” Ammachi set the plate down and patted Indu's shoulder. “Such good manners. In my father's house we stood too. Now my knees are old, so everyone sits!” Usha stopped giggling. “So it's not weird?” “Different houses, different ways,” said Ammachi. “Both are respect.” Indu grinned and took a chip.

qa.q: What did Ammachi bring in?
qa.a: Ammachi brought a plate of banana chips.

qa.q: Why were Indu's cheeks warm after sitting back down?
qa.a: Indu felt embarrassed when Usha giggled, worried the habit of standing looked strange in this house.

qa.q: How did Ammachi help both children?
qa.a: She praised Indu's manners, shared that her own family once stood too and said both ways are respect, so no one felt wrong.

qa.q: How might Usha feel after Ammachi's words?
qa.a: Usha probably felt a little sheepish and more understanding, seeing that standing up was a family custom, not something weird.

grounding: Shows a child standing when an elder enters as respect, and how such rules differ between families.

passage: I'm Harsha, and when I started karate last year, the first thing Nirmala Sensei taught us wasn't a kick. It was the bow: feet together, hands at our sides, bend from the waist before stepping on the mat, and kneel in a line at the end. The first time, I felt silly. When I showed my friends at school, Kunal laughed. “You bow to her? That's so weak.” I didn't know what to say. At the next class I asked Sensei. She said, “We bow to say thank you for the teaching, and to the mat for keeping us safe. Strong people show respect.” Now I bow without feeling silly at all.

qa.q: What did Nirmala Sensei teach first?
qa.a: She taught the bow first, not a kick.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel the first time bowing?
qa.a: Harsha felt silly and self-conscious, and later unsure what to say when Kunal called it weak.

qa.q: What did Harsha do after being teased, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Harsha asked Sensei what the bow meant, which gave a real reason to feel proud instead of silly.

qa.q: Why might Kunal see bowing as weak?
qa.a: Kunal may not know that in karate the bow means thanks and respect, so he read it as giving in.

grounding: Shows a child learning to bow and kneel in a karate class as respect, not weakness, with rules differing between settings.

passage: Class note, Friday. Jaya, Grade 5. Kashish joined us from a school in Varanasi this week. Every time a teacher enters, she stands up straight beside her desk, as her old school taught. Nobody else here does. Today two boys started standing up and sitting down to mock her, and Kashish went scarlet and stayed seated all afternoon, eyes down. At the end of the day I spoke to the class: “In many schools and homes, standing when an elder enters is respect. Here we don't need to, but it's never wrong.” I told Kashish privately she can stand or sit, whichever feels right. I spoke to the two boys before they left.

qa.q: Where did Kashish come from?
qa.a: Kashish came from a school in Varanasi.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when she stayed seated all afternoon?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and ashamed after being mocked for standing, so she hid a habit she had been proud of.

qa.q: How did Jaya respect both sets of school rules?
qa.a: Jaya explained to the class that standing is respect elsewhere, told Kashish privately she could choose, and dealt with the mocking boys the same day.

qa.q: How might the two boys see standing up after Jaya spoke?
qa.a: They might realise it was a sign of respect from another school, not something odd to mock.

grounding: Shows a child standing when teachers enter as respect, and how such rules differ across schools.

passage:
Wednesday

New school, day three. When Sarita Ma'am walks in, the whole class jumps up and says, "Good mooorning, Ma'am!" At my old school in Bengaluru we just stayed sitting and waved. On the first day I was the only one still in my chair, and my face went hot.

Today Ali, who came from Dubai last year, whispered, "Standing up feels like we're scared of her." I told him it's not scared, it's like when I touch Ajoba's feet before an exam. It's respect. He said at his house they kiss their grandfather's hand instead. So we worked out that everybody's respect looks different. I stood up fastest today!

Nilesh

qa.q: Where was Nilesh's old school?
qa.a: In Bengaluru.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel on the first day, as the only one still sitting?
qa.a: Embarrassed and out of place, as the hot face shows, since Nilesh did not yet know the new rule.

qa.q: What helped Nilesh and Ali understand each other's customs?
qa.a: They compared what respect looks like at home, touching Ajoba's feet and kissing a grandfather's hand, instead of judging each other's habits.

qa.q: How did Ali first see the class standing up?
qa.a: Ali felt it looked like being scared of the teacher, because it was not a custom he knew.

grounding: It is a child's diary about standing when a teacher enters and touching an elder's feet as respect, and learning that such customs differ between families and schools.
